paper.title: Predicting acute radiation esophagitis after lung cancer radiotherapy: Clinical-DVH model development and incremental evaluation of deep-learning-derived dose features.
paper.abstract: To develop and evaluate a clinical-dose-volume histogram (DVH) model for predicting grade ≥2 acute radiation esophagitis after lung cancer radiotherapy and to assess the incremental predictive information provided by deep-learning-derived dose features. This retrospective study expanded a previously reported cohort to 414 patients from Fuzhou Pulmonary Hospital of Fujian Province (Center A) and The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xiamen Medical College (Xiamen Second Hospital; Center B). Clinical predictor stability and 15 DVH metrics were assessed in 228 patients in the development cohort. The resulting clinical-DVH reference model was compared with 2 extended models incorporating either global or 4-bin longitudinal deep dose features extracted from the same 3-dimensional dose region using the same pretrained encoder with frozen weights. After selection of the clinical-DVH specification, preprocessing and ridge regression were performed within a nested cross-validation framework. The models were then evaluated without refitting in an earlier Center B cohort (n = 86) and a later Center B cohort (n = 100), which together included 110 patients not included in the previous publication. Age met the stability criterion in 91 of 100 splits. Among the clinical-DVH combinations evaluated, age plus V40 ranked highest, with a mean held-out area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.821. In the subsequent matched comparison, out-of-fold AUCs were 0.809, 0.801, and 0.787 for the reference model, global fusion, and longitudinal fusion, respectively. Corresponding AUCs in the earlier/later Center B cohorts were 0.725/0.713, 0.750/0.728, and 0.777/0.732. In the earlier/later Center B cohorts, longitudinal fusion reduced Brier scores from 0.207/0.201 to 0.174/0.178, respectively. Among the 110 additional Center B patients not included in the previous publication, its AUC point estimate was 0.635, compared with 0.576 for the reference model. Absolute risks remained overestimated, and paired bootstrap intervals for AUC differences included zero. Development-cohort analyses supported age plus V40 as a parsimonious reference model. Deep-learning-derived dose features showed potential to add predictive information at Center B, particularly with longitudinal pooling. Independent validation and further assessment of calibration are warranted.

paper.title: Explainable Machine Learning for Predicting Incident Heart Failure from Routine Electronic Health Record Data.
paper.abstract:
Background: Heart failure (HF) is largely preventable. Contemporary therapies can reduce incident HF among at-risk individuals, making scalable and accurate identification of high-risk patients a priority. Risk prediction models are traditionally developed from long-term epidemiologic cohorts, but machine learning (ML) can derive interpretable models directly from electronic health record (EHR) data captured in routine care. We developed an interpretable ML model for incident HF from health-system EHR data and compared it with established risk equations.
Methods: We developed ML-based models for 5-year incident HF using EHR data from the Stanford Healthcare system, incorporating over 2000 predictors including structured data, temporal transformations, and variable interactions. We applied a neural additive model that combines feature selection and nonparametric survival analysis to develop the AIHF-Base model. We removed implausible predictors in an adjusted model (AIHF-Refined) to enhance clinical interpretability. We internally validated the models using a holdout Stanford sample and externally validated them in an independent national Veterans Affairs (VA) cohort with 10-year follow-up. Model discrimination was compared between the AIHF models and two benchmark HF prediction models, PCP-HF and PREVENT-HF.
Results: The AIHF-Base model achieved an AUC of 0.847 in the Stanford cohort and 0.750 in the VA cohort. The AIHF-Refined model had an AUC of 0.840 (Stanford) and 0.741 (VA). Discrimination was comparable to that of PREVENT-HF and PCP-HF in both cohorts; in the VA cohort the AUC was 0.764 for PREVENT-HF and 0.738 for PCP-HF. Of the 14 features in the AIHF-Refined model, representing 13 distinct clinical variables, 7 used longitudinal EHR data. Age and smoking were the only features used by all models. Of 27 total features across models, 8 were used in at least one AIHF and one benchmark model, 19 were used only by AIHF or benchmark models.
Conclusions: Interpretable ML models built from routine EHR data identified clinically coherent predictors of incident HF and achieved discrimination comparable to established risk equations. By drawing on data already captured in clinical care, including longitudinal trends, this approach offers a scalable, transparent strategy for identifying patients at risk for HF and targeting them for prevention.

paper.title: Deep Learning-Based BNP and NT-proBNP Evaluation From Wearable-Compatible Single-Lead ECGs for Heart Failure Assessment.
paper.abstract:
Background: Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) and N-terminal pro-BNP (NT-proBNP) are critical biomarkers for diagnosing and managing heart failure. With the growing availability of wearable technologies, single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) images have emerged as a practical and noninvasive source of clinical information. This study explores the use of a deep learning-based approach to estimate BNP and NT-proBNP levels from single-lead ECG images, aiming to support rapid, noninvasive screening in real-world settings.
Methods: We analyzed 528,654 lead I ECGs from 237,686 unique patients within the Houston Methodist Health System, each paired with a corresponding BNP value obtained within 24 hours. A modified VGG16 convolutional neural network (CNN) was trained to classify BNP levels into clinically relevant thresholds: ≥100, ≥400, and ≥900 pg/mL. To prevent data leakage and ensure patient-level independence, the dataset was split by unique patients into training, validation, and testing sets. Additionally, the model's generalizability was evaluated by using an external Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)-IV-ECG testing cohort comprising 18,549 unique patients and 42,377 electrocardiograms (ECGs) with corresponding NT-proBNP measurements, with predictions assessed against established NT-proBNP thresholds of ≥125, ≥450, and ≥900 pg/mL. We then examined the association between ECG-predicted BNP (ECG-BNP) and incident HF in 706,715 patients at Houston Methodist.
Results: In the testing dataset, the model demonstrated robust performance, with area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) values ranging from 0.84-0.86 and from 0.79-0.85 across the 3 classification thresholds of BNP and NT-proBNP, respectively. For the prediction of severe BNP elevation (≥900 pg/mL), the model achieved a sensitivity of 0.87 and a specificity of 0.70. The overall accuracy for distinguishing normal (<100 pg/mL) from elevated BNP levels (ie, ≥100 pg/mL) was 0.76. For NT-proBNP, the discriminative ability was higher at the lower cutoff (≥125 pg/mL) and declined slightly as thresholds increased, with AUROC values of 0.85, 0.82, and 0.79 for ≥125, ≥450, and ≥900 pg/mL, respectively. Consistent performance was observed across various demographic groups (sex and age categories) for all BNP and NT-proBNP thresholds. Higher baseline ECG-derived BNP levels were retrospectively associated with subsequent HF diagnosis across follow-up intervals extending up to 10 years, with stronger associations observed among patients whose baseline ECGs were temporally closer to HF diagnosis.
Conclusion: This study developed and validated a deep-learning model for classifying clinically relevant BNP and NT-proBNP thresholds from single-lead ECG images. The model demonstrated strong discrimination and external validation, supporting further investigation of single-lead ECG-derived natriuretic peptide classification for scalable cardiovascular screening and risk assessment.

paper.title: Leveraging Large Language Models to Understand Reasons for SGLT2 Nontreatment Among Patients With Heart Failure.
paper.abstract:
Background: Many patients with heart failure (HF) and a guideline indication for sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) do not receive a prescription, but the reasons behind this are unclear. This study optimizes an large language model framework to identify reasons for the lack of SGLT2i prescriptions.
Methods And Results: We extracted clinical notes for patients >18 years old with a first HF diagnosis identified by International Classification of Diseases, 10th edition, code seen in cardiology clinics between August 10, 2021, and March 1, 2025. Five annotators labeled reasons for SGLT2i nonprescription (the test set); the remaining unlabeled notes served as the inference set. Using both zero-shot (prompts do not include examples) and few-shot prompting techniques, we compared 2 large language models from OpenAI on their ability to classify the documented reason for nonprescription into 1 of 6 themes and 1 of 14 subthemes. We identified 599 HF patients (with 1123 notes), with an average age of 71 years and predominantly having HF with preserved ejection fraction. We used 313 labeled and 705 unlabeled notes as the test and inference sets, respectively, for a total set of 1018 notes. GPT-o1 outperformed GPT-4o and was 84.7% accurate (95% confidence interval 80.2%-88.5%) in identifying theme reasons for SGLT2i nonprescription. The most frequent theme was physician-attributed factors (n = 292 notes [28.7%]), among the total set. Physician deferral to a future visit (n = 157 notes [15.4%]) and the physician perceiving the patient to be at low risk or unlikely to benefit (n = 75 [7.4%]) were the most prevalent subthemes.
Conclusions: We optimized a large language model to accurately discriminate reasons for not prescribing SGLT2is from clinical notes. When a reason for SGLT2i nonprescription was documented, delayed initiation of SGLT2i and physician perception of patients as being at low risk were the most common reasons, offering valuable insight to improve guideline-indicated SGLT2i prescription.

paper.title: Automated Deep Learning Pipeline for Characterizing Left Ventricular Diastolic Function.
paper.abstract:
Introduction: Left ventricular diastolic dysfunction (LVDD) is most commonly evaluated by echocardiography. However, without a sole identifying metric, LVDD is assessed by a diagnostic algorithm relying on secondary characteristics that is laborious and has the potential for interobserver variability.
Methods: To characterize concordance in clinical evaluations of LVDD, we evaluated historical echocardiogram studies at 2 academic medical centers for variability between clinical diastology reported by clinicians and the 2016 and 2025 American Society of Echocardiography (ASE) guidelines. We developed a workflow of 8 deep learning (DL) models trained on over 155,000 studies to automate LVDD assessment. Model performance was evaluated on held-out test sets from 3 academic centers.
Results: In 592 studies from Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (CSMC), DL demonstrated 80.4% agreement and a weighted Cohen kappa of 0.62 with the 2016 ASE guideline assessment. In contrast, the CSMC clinician evaluation had 52.2% agreement and a kappa of 0.46 with the 2016 guidelines. In the Stanford Healthcare (SHC) cohort of 1572 studies, DL had 66.7% agreement and a kappa of 0.33 with the 2016 guidelines vs clinical diastology, with 32.7% agreement and a kappa of 0.14. Our DL workflow showed strong concordance with the 2025 guidelines, with agreements of 81.8% in CSMC and 68.1% in SHC. In a third validation cohort of 204 studies from the University of Chicago, DL had 34.3% agreement with the 2025 guidelines.
Conclusions: Evaluating LVDD has high heterogeneity. We developed DL measurement-driven diastolic dysfunction, a pipeline of models that automates the clinical workflow of grading LVDD and can contribute to improved diagnosis of heart failure.

paper.title: A multicenter-validated machine learning model for predicting in-hospital mortality in ICU patients with cirrhosis.
paper.abstract:
Background: Intensive care unit (ICU) patients with cirrhosis face a high in-hospital mortality risk. We aimed to develop and externally validate an interpretable machine learning model for early mortality prediction using routinely collected variables from the first 24 hours of ICU admission.
Methods: In this multicenter retrospective cohort study, the model was developed and internally validated on the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU) and externally validated on Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV (MIMIC-IV), Northwestern ICU (NWICU), and Shenzhen People's Hospital (SZPH). The primary outcome was all-cause in-hospital mortality. Features selected by LASSO were used to build an XGBoost model. Performance was evaluated by AUROC and Brier score, with calibration curves and decision curve analysis, and compared with five established scores (MELD, MELD-Na, Child-Pugh, SOFA, CLIF-SOFA) and logistic regression using DeLong's tests. SHAP provides interpretable feature attribution.
Results: We included 3,891 patients with cirrhosis (eICU, n=1,870; MIMIC-IV, n=1,697; NWICU, n=134; SZPH, n=190); in-hospital mortality rates were 19.79%, 28.76%, 38.81%, and 47.37%, respectively. The final model used 10 predictors (prothrombin time, mechanical ventilation, creatinine, mean arterial pressure, lactate, respiratory rate, total bilirubin, oxygen saturation, heart rate, and white blood cell count). It showed good discrimination and calibration internally (AUROC 0.814; Brier 0.125) and generalized to external cohorts (AUROCs 0.781, 0.733, and 0.719 in MIMIC-IV, NWICU, and SZPH, respectively). In MIMIC-IV cohort, XGBoost significantly outperformed MELD-Na, Child-Pugh, and SOFA, while differences versus MELD, CLIF-SOFA, and logistic regression were not significant. In eICU internal validation cohort, XGBoost significantly outperformed Child-Pugh and SOFA but not other comparators; in SZPH cohort, it showed comparable discrimination to all comparators.
Conclusion: We developed and multicenter-validated an interpretable XGBoost model predicting in-hospital mortality in ICU patients with cirrhosis, with competitive or superior discrimination versus established scores. Prospective validation, local recalibration, and implementation studies are warranted.

paper.title: Development of a Multimodal Model Combining Imaging and Clinical Data to Predict Bone Cement Leakage During Vertebroplasty for Fresh Thoracolumbar Compression Fractures.
paper.abstract:
Background: Bone cement leakage is a common complication of percutaneous vertebroplasty (PVP), but perioperative risk stratification remains challenging. Existing models based on single-source clinical or imaging features have limited performance. This study aimed to develop and validate multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) models integrating clinical, imaging, and radiomics features to predict bone cement leakage during PVP.
Methods: This multicenter study included 486 treated vertebrae from 378 patients at the North, South, and Shenshan campuses of our hospital. The treated vertebra was the prediction unit, while all vertebrae from the same patient were retained in the same dataset partition and cross-validation fold. Clinical variables, conventional CT imaging features, and CT-based radiomics features were extracted. Logistic regression identified independent risk factors. Six machine-learning algorithms were used to construct clinical, imaging, radiomics, and multimodal models. Performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, F1 score, and decision curve analysis. Independent external and prospective validations were performed, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used for model interpretation.
Results: Among the 486 treated vertebrae, 215 (44.2%) had cement leakage. Higher body mass index (BMI), greater cement injection volume, cortical destruction, and posterior wall involvement were independently associated with leakage. Multimodal models generally achieved higher AUCs than the corresponding single-modality models, with AUCs of 0.902-0.939 in the internal test cohort, 0.722-0.929 in the external validation cohort, and 0.834-0.925 in the prospective validation cohort. Patient-level aggregation and one-vertebra-per-patient sensitivity analyses yielded broadly comparable discrimination. SHAP identified cortical destruction, cement injection volume, and posterior wall involvement as the most influential predictors.
Conclusions: The multimodal models demonstrated good and generally consistent discrimination across the internal test, external validation, and prospective validation cohorts and may support perioperative risk assessment and individualized cement injection planning during PVP.

paper.title: Development and validation of a machine learning-based combined model for malignancy risk prediction in pulmonary subsolid nodules: a dual-center study.
paper.abstract:
Background: Accurate characterization of pulmonary subsolid nodules (SSNs) is important for selecting surveillance, biopsy, or surgery. Existing clinical models were developed in broader nodule populations and may not fully reflect the radiological and biological features of SSNs.
Methods: This dual-center retrospective study included 225 patients with pathologically confirmed SSNs from January 2018 to January 2024. The development center contributed 167 patients, split into internal training (n = 118) and internal validation (n = 49) cohorts, and the external center contributed 58 patients. Ten machine-learning algorithms were compared within the development cohort. The final combined model used four routinely available predictors: spiculation, consolidation-to-tumor ratio (CTR), CYFRA 21 - 1, and nodule diameter. Discrimination, calibration, decision-curve analysis, pairwise model comparison, and sensitivity analyses were performed.
Results: The combined model achieved AUCs of 0.932 (95% CI, 0.887-0.977), 0.954 (95% CI, 0.895-1.000), and 0.930 (95% CI, 0.864-0.995) in the internal training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. In external validation, the corresponding AUCs for the Mayo, VA, Brock, and PKUPH models were 0.750, 0.560, 0.800, and 0.840. Calibration was evaluated in all three cohorts, and decision-curve analysis showed net benefit across threshold probabilities of approximately 0.12-0.68 in external validation.
Conclusions: A four-variable combined model integrating imaging features and CYFRA 21 - 1 showed consistent discrimination across the internal and external validation cohorts. The web calculator may support research-stage risk estimation, but prospective multicenter validation is needed before clinical implementation.

paper.title: Application of artificial intelligence-assisted ultrasound in the segmentation of splenic trauma.
paper.abstract:
Objectives: To develop an artificial intelligence(AI)-assisted ultrasound segmentation model for splenic trauma and to evaluate its clinical utility for trauma localization and contour delineation.
Methods: (1) We assembled an animal ultrasound dataset comprising 4,280 images and a clinical dataset comprising 117 cases (318 human ultrasound images) of splenic trauma. Among the clinical images, 123 were used as a training set to adapt the baseline animal-trained model. The remaining clinical images were used for independent evaluation: 77 splenic trauma images collected at the Chinese People's Liberation Army General Hospital served as the internal test set, and 118 images collected at the Beijing Chaoyang Emergency Rescue Center served as the external test set. (2) Lesion segmentation and contour delineation were independently performed by three senior ultrasound physicians (each with at least 15 years of experience). The physicians manually outlined splenic trauma lesions as precisely as possible, using contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) and/or contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) as the reference standard when available. (3) We applied transfer learning to fine-tune the animal-trained model using the human splenic trauma dataset. For performance comparison, three ultrasound physicians with different experience levels (a junior physician with two years of standardized training, an intermediate physician with five years of clinical ultrasound experience, and a senior physician with ten years of clinical ultrasound experience) independently assessed splenic trauma, and their results were compared with the artificial intelligence outputs.
Results: (1) The Dice coefficients for AI and ultrasound physicians of different seniority in Internal Test Set and External Test Set were as follows: Internal Test Set: 0.71, 0.79, 0.79, and 0.79; External Test Set: 0.74, 0.76, 0.77, and 0.79. (2) Across different American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST)grades, the AI Dice coefficients were higher than those of junior and intermediate physicians for AAST grade II (Internal Test Set: 0.71 vs. 0.68 and 0.67; External Test Set: 0.76 vs. 0.73 and 0.74) and AAST grade III (Internal Test Set: 0.75 vs. 0.71 and 0.72; External Test Set: 0.76 vs. 0.70 and 0.72) and were closer to the performance of senior physicians. (3) For stratified analyses by AAST grade, AI and senior physicians showed greater reproducibility between Internal Test Set and External Test Set than junior and intermediate physicians.
Conclusion: AI demonstrated strong performance for ultrasound-based segmentation of splenic trauma and maintained stable diagnostic consistency across test sets and injury grades.

paper.title: A multi-task deep learning framework incorporating tumor morphology for MRI-based MGMT methylation prediction in glioblastoma.
paper.abstract:
Background: Methylation of the O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter is a clinically important biomarker associated with prognosis and treatment response in glioblastoma. However, its assessment typically requires invasive tissue sampling. This study aimed to develop and validate a non-invasive, MRI-based deep learning model for MGMT methylation prediction, incorporating tumor morphological information through a multi-task learning (MTL) framework.
Methods: We developed a deep learning model that jointly performs tumor segmentation and MGMT methylation classification. The model was trained on a publicly available cohort from The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) and independently validated in an institutional cohort of patients with glioblastoma. Multiparametric MRI sequences, including contrast-enhanced T1-weighted and T2-FLAIR images, were used. Three input strategies were evaluated: image-only, image combined with tumor mask, and an MTL framework integrating segmentation and classification. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).
Results: Among the evaluated convolutional neural network architectures, the ConvNeXt-V2-based MTL model demonstrated the best performance. It achieved an AUC of 0.862 in development-cohort cross-validation and 0.769 in independent institutional validation. The MTL approach incorporating tumor morphological information consistently outperformed image-only and image-plus-mask models, particularly in the independent institutional validation cohort, suggesting improved generalizability.
Conclusions: An MRI-based multi-task deep learning model integrating tumor segmentation and classification shows promising performance for non-invasive MGMT methylation prediction in glioblastoma. Incorporation of morphological information through an MTL framework may enhance model robustness across datasets, particularly under limited data conditions. This approach may provide complementary information for non-invasive molecular profiling and support clinical decision-making in glioblastoma.

paper.title: Pre-treatment T2WI-based automated artificial intelligence system for predicting neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy response and prognosis in locally advanced rectal cancer: a multicenter study.
paper.abstract:
Background: In clinical practice, approximately 15-25% of patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) achieve a pathological complete response (pCR), defined as tumor regression grade 0 according to the AJCC 8th edition, which is closely associated with favorable prognosis. However, noninvasive and accurate preoperative assessment methods remain a major clinical challenge. We aimed to develop an automated artificial intelligence (AI) system for predicting the response to neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and prognosis in LARC using pre-treatment T2WI.
Methods: This multicenter retrospective study included 227 LARC patients from Center 1 as the development cohort and 72 and 55 patients from two separate centers as external validation cohorts 1 and 2, respectively. 3D Swin-UNETR was constructed to automatically identify LARC tumors. Based on the segmented tumor volumes, three analytical approaches were implemented to support downstream tasks. Specifically, 1,132 radiomic features (Rf) were extracted using PyRadiomics, while 2,048 deep learning features (Dlf) were derived by 3D ResNet-152 architecture. Following a series of feature selection steps, predictive response scores were generated, including RF scores (Rfs) and Dlf scores (Dlfs). Additionally, an end-to-end analysis was performed to automatically generate Dl scores (Dls). A multi-perspective feature engineering model was then developed by integrating Rfs, Dlfs, and Dls. The predictive performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUROCs). Prognostic indices, including disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS), were assessed using Kaplan-Meier (KM) analysis, with the Log-Rank test used to compare KM curves.
Results: The fusion model achieved moderate AUROCs of 0.756 and 0.751 in external validation cohorts 1 and 2, respectively. It effectively stratified OS risk, with p-values < 0.05 across all cohorts. For DFS, statistical significance was inconsistent across cohorts, being achieved in the development cohort (p = 0.0084) and external cohort 2 (p = 0.044), but not in external cohort 1 (p = 0.068). These findings are exploratory and require prospective confirmation.
Conclusions: The proposed AI system demonstrates moderate, externally validated performance for assessing treatment response and OS risk stratification in LARC and may serve as a decision-support tool to assist clinical judgment.

paper.title: Biparametric MRI with deep learning for the preoperative prediction of muscle invasion in patients with bladder cancer: a multicenter study.
paper.abstract:
Objectives: This study aimed to develop and validate a deep learning model that integrates T2-weighted imaging (T2WI) and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) for the noninvasive prediction of muscle invasion in bladder cancer.
Materials And Methods: A total of 308 bladder tumors from 254 patients were retrospectively collected from three institutions. Of these, 177 tumors from Center 1 were partitioned via stratified sampling into a training set (n = 128) and an internal validation set (n = 49). The remaining two centers contributed 59 and 72 tumors, respectively, which served as external validation cohorts. A dual-branch 3D deep convolutional neural network (Joint model) based on biparametric MRI (bp-MRI) was developed using the training data and compared with a deep learning model based on T2WI (T2WI model) and VI-RADS assessments by radiologists. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity.
Results: The Joint model achieved mean AUCs of 0.979 ± 0.007 in the internal validation cohort, and 0.907 ± 0.013 and 0.916 ± 0.021 in the external validation cohorts. It outperformed the T2WI model in all cohorts and achieved higher AUCs than radiologists across all validation cohorts. Notably, for equivocal VI-RADS 2-3 lesions, the Joint model yielded higher accuracy than the T2WI model in external validation.
Conclusion: Compared with the T2WI model and VI-RADS assessment, the Joint model demonstrated better diagnostic performance and generalizability for predicting muscle invasion in patients with bladder cancer.
Key Points: Question Reliable noninvasive tools for preoperative prediction of muscle invasion in bladder cancer are lacking, as TURBT-based staging carries procedural risks and frequent understaging. Findings A biparametric MRI deep learning model achieved AUCs of 0.907-0.979 across internal and external validation cohorts, outperforming T2WI-only models and VI-RADS. Critical relevance statement Contrast-free biparametric MRI combined with deep learning enables accurate, generalizable preoperative prediction of muscle invasion, offering particular value for equivocal VI-RADS 2-3 lesions and supporting noninvasive clinical decision-making.
